title: Rama's promise: do not fear
hookLine: Ravana's own brother crosses to Rama's camp, and Rama makes a vow the raised palm still keeps
carry: abhaya: the god's promise to anyone who comes
tomorrow: why did Brahma make a fifth Veda?

cards: Before the war, while Rama's army waits on the shore, a figure comes across the sea to Rama's camp. It's Vibhishana, younger brother of Ravana, the king who stole Sita.

He begged his brother to give her back, and was thrown out for it. Now he hangs in the sky above the monkey army and asks for refuge. Below him, Sugriva, the monkey king, says what everyone is thinking.
It's a trick. He's Ravana's brother. He's a spy.

teach.b: Rama hears out the whole camp. Some say test him first; Hanuman says his face shows no deceit.
Then Rama answers, in Valmiki's Ramayana, here in paraphrase: to anyone who comes to me even once and says, I am yours, I give fearlessness from all beings. That is my vow. Bring him in.
Even if it were Ravana himself. The word Rama uses for that gift is abhayam: fearlessness. Now stand before a temple image, Shiva dancing, Durga, Rama himself.
One hand is raised, open, palm toward you, fingers up.

teach.h: ABHAYA MUDRA: THE GIFT OF FEARLESSNESS.
teach.b: That's abhaya mudra, the gesture of that same gift: do not be afraid.
Often a second hand hangs low, palm open, fingers down: varada mudra, the hand that grants what is asked. Here's the teaching.
In Hindu devotion, turning to God even once, even from the wrong side of the war, is enough to be taken in.
Teachers call that turning sharanagati, taking refuge, and many Vaishnava teachers count Rama's vow among its great promises. So the raised palm isn't decoration, and it isn't stop.

teach.h: A PROMISE STANDING IN THE ROOM.
teach.b: It's a promise standing in the room. That's why frightened people, before surgery, before an exam, before a first day, go and stand in front of it.
The Gita adds one more layer: in its sixteenth chapter, the list of qualities that lean toward the divine begins with the same word, abhayam.
Many teachers read the palm both ways: a promise of protection, and a fearlessness meant to grow in the one who looks.

how: Devotees meet abhaya and varada mudras on the images of deities in temples and home shrines; the raised open palm is read as "do not fear" and the lowered open palm as the giving of blessings. Many pray before them when they are afraid, and Sri Vaishnava teachers cite Rama's vow to Vibhishana as a great promise of refuge (sharanagati).

games.q: a friend hasn't been to temple in years: 'they'll all know i'm a fake.' by Rama's vow, what fits?
o: turning toward God even once is enough to be taken in.
she should wait until she's been good for a while.

games.why: Rama took in Ravana's own brother: to anyone who comes even once and says 'i am yours', fearlessness. the raised palm holds out the same promise.

practice: Let the left hand rest beside the left knee, palm open and turned forward, fingers down: the giving hand. Raise the right hand to shoulder height, palm forward, fingers relaxed: do not fear.
Breathe slowly, and if a worry comes, let it meet the raised palm without arguing. If you pray, face a home shrine and say silently, I am yours. If not, just rest in the two shapes.

wordCard.voice: The mudras. Today, two you receive: abhaya, the raised palm that says do not fear, and varada, the low open hand that gives.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: abhaya, fearlessness. Abhayam opens the list of divine qualities in Gita 16.
